8.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what do you ask a knee patient?"
- "Pain, swelling, locking, giving way, then stiffness, deformity and function."
- "The injury: contact or not, which way it twisted, swelling at once or next day."
- "Can he still play? Then past history, other joints, red flags."

### Pain — where and when
| Pain | Think of |
|---|---|
| Localised | meniscus |
| Diffuse | degenerative |
| During activity | ACL or meniscus |
| After activity | inflammation, tendinitis |
| Going uphill | tibiofemoral joint |
| Going downhill | patellofemoral joint |
| Morning stiffness | OA, inflammatory arthritis |

- ACL = anterior cruciate ligament; OA = osteoarthritis
- Kneeling, squatting → patellofemoral pain
- Think of pain referred from the hip or spine

### Swelling — the clock matters
- At once (first hour) → blood; next morning → reactive effusion

| At once (blood) | Next day (effusion) |
|---|---|
| ACL tear | meniscal tear |
| Patellar dislocation | serous effusion |
| Peripheral meniscal tear | cartilage injury |
| Intra-articular fracture | |

- Torn ACL causes 65–70% of acute post-traumatic haemarthroses (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- Painless haemarthrosis → capsule torn, fluid escapes; bigger injury (Exam Techniques)
- **Memory:** blood at once = ACL until proved otherwise

### Giving way, locking, catching
- Never accept "yes" or "no" to "does it give way?"

| Symptom | Means | Causes |
|---|---|---|
| Straight giving way | knee buckles | extensor mechanism: weak quadriceps, rupture, patella fracture |
| Rotatory giving way | "something slips inside" | ACL deficiency |
| True locking | block to full extension | loose body, bucket-handle tear, ACL stump |
| Catching (pseudo-locking) | brief, frees itself | pain inhibition, patellofemoral |
| Going out | patella slips out | patellar instability |

- True locking loses the last 10–20° of extension (Nagah)

[[FIG: Fig 8.1 — Locked knee: tenderness over a displaced bucket-handle tear · 8.01

### The injury story
- Contact or not? Direction of the twist? Could he finish the game?

#### Ask every time
| Complaint | Ask |
|---|---|
| Pain | where? during or after activity? night? |
| Swelling | at once or next day? recurrent? |
| Instability | buckling or rotatory slip? going out? |
| Mechanical | true locking or catching? |
| Function | sport level, stairs, squatting, work |
| Past | surgery, injections, other joints |

- **Red flags:** constant or night pain → tumour or infection
- **Memory:** four knee words — pain, swelling, locking, giving way
- General interview → ch 1

8.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "examine this knee"
- "Standing: look front, side, behind; walk; sitting: patella tracking."
- "Supine: look, feel effusion and joint lines, move, then ligaments in fixed order."
- "Prone: dial test; then neurovascular, hip and ankle."

- **Whole knee exam (video):** [▶ Dr James Gill · 4:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oyKH4EYfJDM)

### The route on one page
| Position | What you do (in order) |
|---|---|
| Standing | Look front, side, behind: alignment, Q angle, recurvatum, FFD, feet |
| Walking | Gait: antalgic, varus or valgus thrust, stiff knee |
| Sitting | Look: patellar height, J sign, crepitus |
| Supine | Look: wasting, scars, swelling; thigh girth |
| Supine | Feel: warmth, effusion, joint lines at 90°; Move: SLR, extension, flexion |
| Supine | Special: sag, quadriceps active, drawers, Lachman, collaterals, menisci, patella |
| Prone | Dial test, Apley, prone hanging |
| Finish | neuro, vascular, nodes, hip, ankle, spine |

- FFD = fixed flexion deformity; SLR = straight leg raise
- **Memory:** Look, Feel, Move, Measure, Special · then Neuro, Vascular, Joints above/below

### Standing and walking
#### Look — front, side, behind
- Expose both legs from mid-thigh, barefoot — never a rolled-up trouser

| View | Look for |
|---|---|
| Front | varus or valgus, Q angle, squinting patellae, wasting, scars |
| Side | FFD, recurvatum |
| Behind | popliteal cyst, scars, heel valgus or varus |
| Feet | flat feet — important in anterior knee pain |

- Say "**attitude**", not deformity, until you have examined it

[[FIG: Fig 8.2 — Standing: valgus, varus, FFD, squinting patellae · 8.02

#### Gait
| Gait | Points to |
|---|---|
| **Antalgic** | painful knee |
| **Varus thrust** | medial OA, lateral laxity, PCL with posterolateral laxity |
| **Valgus thrust** | lateral compartment collapse, medial laxity |
| **Stiff knee** | tibiofemoral pain or weak quadriceps |

- PCL = posterior cruciate ligament
- **Memory:** thrust goes toward the side that has collapsed or opened

[[FIG: Fig 8.3 — Varus thrust on loading the right leg · 8.02

### Sitting
- Legs hanging over the couch edge
- Look: patellar height; active extension → J sign (8.4); feel crepitus

[[FIG: Fig 8.4 — Sitting: height, tracking, crepitus · 8.02

### Supine
#### Look
- Head down on the pillow, hands on the chest
- Roll under the knee: slight flexion, back in view

| Look for | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Vastus medialis wasting | first muscle to waste; chronic problem |
| Quadriceps scar | explains a knee that will not bend |
| Diffuse swelling | effusion; localised → bursa, cyst (8.3) |

[[FIG: Fig 8.5 — Surface anatomy, front of the knee · 8.02

#### Feel
- Warmth with the back of the hand, both knees
- Effusion tests next (8.3)
- Then knee to 90°, foot flat; painless side first

| Feel (knee at 90°) | Tender → think of |
|---|---|
| Medial joint line, posteromedial | medial meniscus tear |
| Lateral joint line | lateral meniscus tear or cyst |
| MCL, femoral attachment | MCL sprain |
| LCL in figure-of-4 | LCL injury |
| Patellar tendon, tibial tubercle | tendinopathy, Osgood–Schlatter |
| Popliteal fossa | cyst, mass, pulse |

- MCL / LCL = medial / lateral collateral ligament
- Infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve crosses just below the patella

[[FIG: Fig 8.6 — Joint line palpated at 90°; LCL felt in figure-of-4 · 8.02

#### Move
- Active SLR first → extensor mechanism intact
- Range: 0° (or −5°) to 135° (Nagah)
- Lift both heels → compare hyperextension

| Finding | Definition |
|---|---|
| FFD | last degrees of extension lost, active and passive |
| Extension lag | active extension lost, passive full |
| Stiffness | all movement lost |

- **Memory:** lag = active only; FFD = both
- Write "10° of hyperextension", never "extension 10°"

[[FIG: Fig 8.7 — SLR, passive extension, heel-to-buttock flexion · 8.02

### Prone and finish
| Step | Do |

| Prone | dial test, Apley test, prone hanging test |
| Neuro | quadriceps (femoral L2–L4), hamstrings (sciatic L5–S2) |
| Vascular | popliteal, dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial pulses |
| Nodes, joints | inguinal nodes, hip, ankle, spine |

- Tight hamstrings hide drawer and Lachman laxity (Kasr Al-Ainy)

8.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "is there an effusion, and how is the alignment?"
- "Small effusion: bulge test. Moderate: patellar tap. Large: cross fluctuation."
- "Standing: varus or valgus, Q angle, recurvatum. Supine: FFD, girth."

### Effusion — which test for how much
- Gutters and pouch full → effusion; gutters empty → local bursa
- Swelling but no fluid → synovial thickening, e.g. pigmented villonodular synovitis (PVNS)

[[FIG: Fig 8.9 — Effusion fills the hollows beside the patella · 8.03

#### Bulge (wipe) test
- **Aim:** small effusion
- **How:** empty the pouch; stroke the medial gutter, then the lateral
- **Positive:** bulge returns on the medial side → small effusion
- **Why:** a little fluid moves between gutters; too much cannot
- **Trap:** negative in a large, tense effusion (McRae)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ySpqA-K5kjo)

[[FIG: Fig 8.10 — Bulge test: stroke one gutter, watch the other · 8.03

#### Patellar tap test
- **Aim:** moderate effusion
- **How:** squeeze the pouch down; push the patella sharply backward
- **Positive:** patella clicks on the femur and floats back → effusion
- **Why:** fluid lifts the patella off the trochlea
- **Trap:** slight or tense effusion → false negative
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=r18O50lzMGw)

[[FIG: Fig 8.11 — Patellar tap: pouch emptied, patella pushed down · 8.03

#### Two-finger displacement test
- **Aim:** small effusion, the course method
- **How:** palm empties the pouch; two light fingers beside the tendon
- **Positive:** the fingers are pushed apart → effusion
- **Why:** the palm works; the fingers only receive (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- **Trap:** eyes on the fingers; no kneading back and forth
- **Video:** [▶ Dr James Gill (effusion tests) · 4:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ruN3d1K7irY)

[[FIG: Fig 8.12 — Course demonstration: palm on the pouch · 8.03

### Alignment — standing
#### Q angle
- **Aim:** quadriceps pull on the patella
- **How:** knee straight; ASIS to patella centre, patella to tubercle
- **Positive:** above about 15° → lateral pull, maltracking (Nagah)
- **Why:** women have a wider pelvis → slightly higher angle
- **Video:** [▶ C Blake · 1:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Murq9XJSKig)

[[FIG: Fig 8.13 — Q angle drawn on the patient and in diagram · 8.03

- ASIS = anterior superior iliac spine

| High Q angle — causes | Level |
|---|---|
| Wide pelvis, genu valgum | above |
| Femoral anteversion | femur |
| External tibial torsion, lateral tubercle | tibia |

- **Memory:** high Q = pelvis wide, femur twisted in, tibia twisted out

#### Varus and valgus
- Normal tibiofemoral angle: about 6° valgus (McRae)
- Intercondylar or intermalleolar gap → ch 11 (11.3)

| Varus knee type | Finding |
|---|---|
| Primary | bony varus only |
| Double | varus + lateral thrust |
| Triple | varus + thrust + recurvatum |

- Correct it by hand: corrects → laxity; fixed → bone or contracture

[[FIG: Fig 8.14 — Varum and valgum; angle and gap · 8.03

#### Recurvatum
- Causes: ACL rupture, tibial growth arrest, laxity, polio, Charcot (McRae)
- Unilateral recurvatum with external rotation → posterolateral corner (8.4)

[[FIG: Fig 8.15 — Hyperextension measured by lifting the heel · 8.03

### Flexion deformity and wasting
#### Prone hanging test
- **Aim:** measure a small knee FFD
- **How:** prone, legs from the knee down over the couch end, relaxed
- **Positive:** heel rests higher → FFD; 1 cm ≈ 1° (Reider)
- **Why:** gravity extends both knees fully; a contracture stops one
- **Video:** [▶ MGH Orthopaedics · 0:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=syHONdwbJuw)

[[FIG: Fig 8.16 — Prone hanging: heel-height difference · 8.03

- Thigh girth → ch 1 (1.4); ≥1 cm = wasting

- Hands moving back and forth like dough prove nothing (Kasr Al-Ainy)

8.04.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "test the ligaments"
- "Sag first, then quadriceps active, drawers, Lachman, collaterals at 0° and 30°."
- "Then dial test, menisci and patella. Sound side first, every test."

- **Memory:** "Sag before drawer" — a sagged tibia fakes an ACL drawer

### Is the PCL torn? (always first)
#### Posterior sag sign
- **Aim:** PCL tear
- **How:** both knees at 90°, heels together; look from the side
- **Positive:** tibial tubercle sags back → PCL torn
- **Why:** the tibia normally steps about 1 cm in front (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- **Video:** [▶ AMBOSS · 1:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wxYY_YmuM8g)

[[FIG: Fig 8.17 — Posterior sag seen from the side · 8.04

#### Quadriceps active test
- **Aim:** confirm a posterior sag
- **How:** knee at 90°, foot held; patient slides the foot forward
- **Positive:** sagged tibia moves forward → PCL torn
- **Why:** quadriceps pulls the tibia through the patellar tendon
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 3:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tQCacgQgC-s)

[[FIG: Fig 8.18 — Quadriceps active test: tibia pulled forward · 8.04

#### Posterior drawer test
- **Aim:** PCL tear, grade it
- **How:** knee at 90°, foot neutral and held; push the tibia back
- **Positive:** backward shift → PCL; 5 mm less step-off = one grade (Reider)
- **Why:** PCL is the main block to backward tibial shift
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wDIGll5wzZs)

[[FIG: Fig 8.19 — Posterior drawer; grade 3 tibia behind the condyles · 8.04

| Posterior grade | Tibia vs femoral condyles |
|---|---|
| Normal | 10 mm in front |
| 1 | 5 mm in front |
| 2 | flush |
| 3 | behind |

### Is the ACL torn?
#### Anterior drawer test (knee)
- **Aim:** ACL tear (anteromedial bundle)
- **How:** knee at 90°, foot held, hamstrings relaxed; pull the tibia forward
- **Positive:** more shift than the sound side, soft end → ACL tear
- **Why:** ACL is the main block to forward shift
- **Trap:** false positive with sag; false negative with spasm, haemarthrosis (Nagah)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 1:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IdnBKv38EEQ)

[[FIG: Fig 8.20 — Anterior drawer at 90°; course and textbook · 8.04

#### Lachman test
- **Aim:** ACL tear — the most sensitive test
- **How:** knee at 20–30°; hold the femur, pull the tibia forward
- **Positive:** more shift, soft or absent end point → ACL tear
- **Why:** at 30° the posterior horn no longer blocks (door-stopper) (Nagah)
- **Trap:** tight hamstrings → false negative; support the thigh (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 2:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JFkbKNNa7xQ)

[[FIG: Fig 8.21 — Lachman; large thigh rested on your knee · 8.04

| Lachman grade | Shift | End point |
|---|---|---|
| 1+ | 3–5 mm | firm |
| 2+ | 6–10 mm | soft |
| 3+ | >10 mm | absent |

#### Pivot shift test
- **Aim:** anterolateral rotatory instability (ACL)
- **How:** knee straight, tibia internally rotated, valgus; flex slowly
- **Positive:** lateral tibia jumps back at about 20° → ACL deficient
- **Why:** extension subluxes the lateral plateau; flexion relocates it (Kasr Al-Ainy)
- **Trap:** painful awake; done under anaesthesia; needs an intact MCL (Nagah)
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 2:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qqy5IfkEvfw)

[[FIG: Fig 8.22 — Pivot shift: valgus and internal rotation, then flexion · 8.04

### Are the collaterals torn?
- Thigh rests on the couch, not lifted

#### Valgus stress test (knee)
- **Aim:** MCL tear
- **How:** valgus push at 0°, then 30°; palpate the medial line
- **Positive:** opens at 30° → MCL; at 0° → plus cruciates
- **Why:** at 30° the capsule and cruciates are slack
- **Video:** [▶ Physiotutors · 2:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GSFbttpxCuQ)

[[FIG: Fig 8.23 — Valgus stress in extension and in flexion · 8.04

| Group | Example |

| Ligament | ACL tear |

| Muscle | quadriceps weakness |
| Pain | patellofemoral pain → reflex inhibition |
